title: Gartner Projects $3.5 Trillion AI Infrastructure Write-Downs by 2030

tickers.name: CoreWeave, Inc. Class A Common Stock

summary:
More than $3.5 trillion of spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure could require write-downs by 2030 because revenue is not expected to cover investment costs, Gartner forecasts. The research firm's analysis suggests that owners of data centers will need approximately $8.5 trillion in revenue by 2030 to earn a 12% return, but it projects actual revenue will only reach $3.6 trillion. This capital gap, which has fueled a recent rout in technology stocks, is likely to result in over 80% of "neocloud" GPU rental providers losing their independence.

Providers are projected to spend $1 trillion on infrastructure in 2026 and another $6 trillion between 2027 and 2030, yet less than half of resulting revenue will reach hardware owners due to the asset-light models of AI app developers. Neoclouds are the most exposed as they lack the diversified revenue streams that allow hyperscalers to absorb such losses. This risk is highlighted by CoreWeave bonds, which yield around 16%, and an AI-optimized infrastructure-as-a-service market that grows from $66 billion in 2027 to $174 billion in 2030, a pace Gartner says is too slow for most providers to recoup investments.

selectedTweets.text:
🦔Gartner figures the owners of AI data centers need about $8.5 trillion in revenue through 2030 to cover their spending and earn a 12% return. Its forecast for the AI revenue tied to those data centers tops out at $3.6 trillion. The research firm puts more than $3.5 trillion of that spending at risk of write-downs and expects over 80% of neoclouds, the companies that rent out AI computing power, to lose their independence by 2030.

My Take
I think we should focus on Gartner’s point that less than half of AI revenue reaches the companies that own the hardware. Customers mostly pay the AI apps, which rent computing power as cheaply as they can. The chip owners end up with the debt and a thin slice of the money, and CoreWeave’s bonds yielding around 16% show us how lenders already see that setup.

Hyperscalers can take a write-down because their other businesses keep paying the bills. Neoclouds have nothing like that to fall back on. In a slow unwind, a hyperscaler or chip supplier probably buys the bigger ones cheaply and their shareholders eat most of the loss. A sudden stop in funding would be uglier, because some would go bankrupt and the losses would spread to bondholders and the private credit funds that paid for their data centers.

Hedgie🤗
